Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

npm preinstall hook executing node setup.mjs (Shai-Hulud dropper) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm's execution stage: a poisoned npm package's 'preinstall':'node setup.mjs' lifecycle hook auto-running the obfuscated dropper the moment a developer runs npm install. Anchored on node.exe launching a script literally named setup.mjs under a package manager parent, which is not a normal legitimate pattern. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact preinstall payload string 'node setup.mjs'; setup.mjs is a non-standard filename and pairing node.exe + this script + a package-manager parent is a high-fidelity, article-specific signature confirmed by Datadog and Unit42 write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/
ATT&CKT1204.003 T1546.016 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal package that genuinely ships a benign preinstall script named setup.mjs (rare but possible in monorepos)
  • Developer intentionally running a project's own setup.mjs build helper via node outside npm
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • CI build agent installing a pinned pre-compromise version whose setup.mjs is a coincidental name
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("lifecycle","run-script") and FolderPath !has "node_modules")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and the enclosing node_modules package path; identify which npm package owns setup.mjs and its version, and check whether it is in the compromised list (keyv, cacheable, flat-cache, file-entry-cache, cache-manager, etc.). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node/bun processes, and immediately rotate any credentials reachable from that dev machine — npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS keys, VAULT_TOKEN. 3) Hunt: search the org for any install of affected package versions, look for child bun.exe execution of Math_Symbol.js and outbound requests to oven-sh/bun releases, and review npm/GitHub audit logs for publishes made with the machine's tokens.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm-cli.js","cmd.exe","sh","bash","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node.exe","yarn","pnpm","cmd.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud payload files setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js written into node_modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the worm's install-stage artifacts: the two new files (setup.mjs dropper and Math_Symbol.js credential-stealer) being written inside a node_modules package directory. Every compromised package in the keyv family gained exactly these two filenames, making them a reliable on-disk indicator. Rationale: Uses the article's two exact dropped filenames (setup.mjs, Math_Symbol.js) constrained to node_modules; both are verbatim from the compromise and cross-confirmed as Shai-Hulud artifacts, giving an extremely low-FP on-disk indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package coincidentally naming a build helper setup.mjs inside its published tarball
  • Local developer git-cloning the compromised repo for analysis (files land on disk without npm install)
  • Backup/AV quarantine tooling re-writing the file path during scanning
  • Monorepo tooling copying package fixtures containing a same-named test file
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the containing package.json to get the package name and version and hash setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js; confirm the version matches a known-poisoned release. 2) Contain: quarantine the files, isolate the host, and delete the affected node_modules; block the package version in the internal registry/proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and CI runners for the same two filenames, check whether Math_Symbol.js was executed (bun child process), and rotate every credential class the payload targets (npm, GitHub, AWS, Vault).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime fetched from oven-sh GitHub releases during npm install AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the worm's C2/staging step: setup.mjs silently downloading the Bun runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/ so it can execute the payload with a runtime other than the local Node. Flags outbound requests to that release path originating from a node/npm/bun process tree. Rationale: Uses the article's exact staging URL path (github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/) tied to a node/npm/bun parent process; a package install that pulls the Bun runtime mid-install is anomalous and specific to this worm. Datadog Sysmon netflow lacks URL paths so that field and Sigma are omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1620 T1102
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI job that legitimately installs Bun as a project runtime/tool
  • Corporate mirror or artifact proxy pre-caching Bun releases
  • Docker base-image builds that fetch Bun as a documented dependency
  • Engineer manually evaluating Bun on their workstation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun upgrade","install bun","setup-bun"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and whether the Bun fetch coincided with an npm install and a setup.mjs execution on the same host within seconds. 2) Contain: if correlated with setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js, isolate the host, terminate bun/node, and rotate exposed credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for bun.exe executing Math_Symbol.js and for outbound HTTP to a Vault endpoint (the payload's Vault token fallback), and review which package version triggered the download.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","bun.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\bun(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*oven-sh/bun/releases/download*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.app Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*oven-sh/bun/releases/download*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.app Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Bun runtime executing Shai-Hulud Math_Symbol.js credential stealer AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access stage: the freshly downloaded Bun runtime executing Math_Symbol.js, the payload that harvests npm tokens from .npmrc, GitHub CLI tokens, AWS keys from ~/.aws/credentials, and the VAULT_TOKEN env var. Using Bun rather than the local Node is a defense-evasion tell, and the script name is verbatim from the campaign. Rationale: Combines the article's exact payload filename (Math_Symbol.js) with its exact evasion runtime (bun); Bun executing a package-dropped JS credential extractor is a near-zero-legitimate pattern and is the direct credential-access step described in the writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1528 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project genuinely running a script named Math_Symbol.js via Bun (extremely unlikely, but possible in a math/symbol-processing library)
  • Malware analyst detonating the payload with Bun in a lab
  • A red-team emulation of the Shai-Hulud chain during an authorized exercise
  • Security tooling replaying the sample for signature testing
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm bun.exe launched Math_Symbol.js and capture the parent chain (npm install -> node setup.mjs -> bun); collect the package name/version. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately and treat all locally reachable secrets as compromised — force-rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs/session/OIDC tokens, AWS access keys and session tokens, and the Vault token; revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: check npm and GitHub audit logs for publishes or repo pushes made with the stolen tokens (worm self-propagation), review AWS CloudTrail for use of the leaked keys, and sweep other dev hosts/CI runners for the same bun+Math_Symbol.js execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-04 15 use cases 6 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Nearly half of C2 malware bypasses DNS by connecting directly to IP addresses. Zero trust IP enforcement secures networks against these threats. The post Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phorpiex staged-payload retrieval from hard-coded C2 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SectopRAT in-browser proxy C2 via /churl endpoint (87.120.107.33 / 194.76.227.94) · [LLM] D2IP / ZT-IP: user-space process direct to public IP with no DNS (WebSocket backdoor 154.92.19.71:39989) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phorpiex staged-payload retrieval from hard-coded C2 178.16.54.109 (no DNS) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoints fetching Phorpiex dropper components directly from the hard-coded IP 178.16.54.109 (st.exe, xmrig.exe, spl.exe, new.php) with no preceding DNS resolution. Article-specific: this IP is a confirmed long-running Phorpiex/Trik C2 that serves staged ransomware/miner payloads over raw HTTP GET. Rationale: 178.16.54.109 is corroborated by Point Wild/Bitsight/Check Point as a live Phorpiex C2 serving st.exe/xmrig.exe/spl.exe; pairing the exact IP with the article's observed payload paths keeps FPs near-zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.pointwild.com/threat-intelligence/phorpiex-inside-the-botnet-powering-global-sextortion-spam-operations/ • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/ransomware-twizt-inside-phorpiex-botnet • https://www.checkpoint.com/cyber-hub/threat-prevention/what-is-malware/phorpiex-malware/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox VM deliberately detonating a Phorpiex sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IP for validation
  • Proxy/IDS replay of a captured PCAP for tuning
  • Honeypot or deception host baiting the C2
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName that opened the socket and whether a payload (st.exe/xmrig.exe/spl.exe) landed on disk via DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 178.16.54.109 at egress, kill the process tree, and quarantine any dropped binary. 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceFileEvents for windrv.exe in %userprofile%, check for XMRig miner processes and scheduled-task/Run-key persistence, and pivot on any other host that resolved-less-connected to the same /24.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "178.16.54.109"
   or (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and RemoteUrl has_any ("178.16.54.109/st.exe","178.16.54.109/xmrig.exe","178.16.54.109/spl.exe","178.16.54.109/new.php","/sex/k/n.txt"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "178.16.54.109"
   or RequestURL has_any ("178.16.54.109/st.exe","178.16.54.109/xmrig.exe","178.16.54.109/spl.exe","178.16.54.109/new.php","/sex/k/n.txt")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

\GET obfuscated exfiltration binary/C2 (SHA256 cc43cdbe / 18.228.188.56) AIexfiltration Medium
Hunts the persistent \GET exfiltration campaign by the known sample hash cc43cdbe... and connections to its Brazil-cloud C2 18.228.188.56. The malware rotates port and IP, so the file hash is the durable anchor; the IP catches un-rotated infrastructure. Rationale: SHA256 cc43cdbe... is the article's named exfil sample and survives the malware's documented IP/port rotation; 18.228.188.56 (AWS Sao Paulo) is the observed \GET C2, so a VPC-flow check is warranted for cloud workloads. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1048 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis lab detonating the sample by hash
  • Shared AWS Sao Paulo tenant IP later reassigned to a benign service (IP clause only)
  • Threat-intel platform test-fetching the C2 to confirm liveness
  • DFIR responder copying the sample between forensic hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which signal fired — hash execution (definitive) vs IP contact (may be shared-cloud reuse). For IP hits, check for a 250–666 char \GET request in proxy logs. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture volatile memory, block 18.228.188.56 and the sample hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: because the actor rotates IP+port, pivot on the sample hash and its parent process across the fleet; review data-egress volume from affected government/airline/university-facing assets for the exfil window.
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where SHA256 == "cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"
   | extend Signal = "KnownExfilBinaryHash"),
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where RemoteIP == "18.228.188.56"
   | extend Signal = "ExfilC2IP")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where TargetFileSHA256 == "cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"
   | extend Signal = "KnownExfilBinaryHash", RemoteIP = ""),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstIpAddr == "18.228.188.56"
   | extend Signal = "ExfilC2IP", TargetFileSHA256 = "", DvcHostname = SrcHostname)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, Signal, TargetFileSHA256, RemoteIP = coalesce(DstIpAddr, RemoteIP), DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_hash="cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

SectopRAT in-browser proxy C2 via /churl endpoint (87.120.107.33 / 194.76.227.94) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts SectopRAT/Arechclient2's browser-mirroring proxy that relays every visited URL to attacker infrastructure via the /churl endpoint, observed against educational institutions on 87.120.107.33 and 194.76.227.94. The /churl path plus these C2 IPs is the article-specific fingerprint. Rationale: SectopRAT's browser-logging/proxy capability is corroborated by Darktrace and G DATA; the /churl relay endpoint plus the two article-reported C2 IPs form a high-fidelity fingerprint distinct from generic RAT beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/not-your-average-rodent-darktraces-mitigation-of-the-sectop-remote-access-trojan-rat • https://www.gdatasoftware.com/blog/2021/02/36633-new-version-adds-encrypted-communication
ATT&CKT1090 T1185 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal API that happens to expose a /churl path (URL-only clause)
  • Pentest/red-team replaying SectopRAT infrastructure in a lab range
  • IP later reassigned to benign hosting after takedown
  • Web-app fuzzing tool generating /churl requests
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "/churl" and RemoteIP !in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process holding the socket (SectopRAT is .NET, often masquerading as a Chrome/installer binary) and confirm whether /churl relayed authenticated session URLs. 2) Contain: isolate host, block both C2 IPs, kill the process, and force-reset credentials for any session the browser had open during the mirror window. 3) Hunt: sweep for the sibling SectopRAT proxy endpoints, .NET loaders in user Temp/AppData, and browser-credential theft; prioritise education-sector assets named in the report.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94")
   or (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and RemoteUrl has "/churl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("87.120.107.33","194.76.227.94")
   or RequestURL has "/churl"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

D2IP / ZT-IP: user-space process direct to public IP with no DNS (WebSocket backdoor 154.92.19.71:39989) AICommand & Control Medium
Operationalises the article's zero-trust-IP thesis: user-writable-path binaries opening outbound public connections with no associated hostname (direct-to-IP), anchored on the hard-coded WebSocket backdoor 154.92.19.71:39989 and C2 2.26.98.67. Surfaces malware that bypasses DNS entirely and is invisible to DNS-based controls. Rationale: Implements the article's ZT-IP methodology: 154.92.19.71:39989 is the Ghidra-confirmed hard-coded WebSocket backdoor address, and the isempty(RemoteUrl) + user-path clause approximates 'no DNS context' for D2IP hunting; the RemoteUrl heuristic is imperfect where the EDR agent omits hostname association, so treat as hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/malware-bypass-dns-direct-to-ip/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • NTP/time-sync clients dialing a hard-coded time-server IP
  • Software auto-updaters that connect to a CDN IP without a fresh lookup (cached hostname)
  • Custom line-of-business apps hard-coding an internal-but-public IP
  • Telemetry/crash-reporter agents in user AppData connecting direct to IP
  • P2P/gaming clients on high non-standard ports
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("w32tm.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","steam.exe","dropbox.exe") and not (RemotePort in (123,80,443) and isempty(RemoteIP) == false and RemoteIP !in ("154.92.19.71","2.26.98.67"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the heuristic hits, confirm the binary is unsigned/user-space and that no DNS query for that IP exists on the host in the prior window; the 154.92.19.71:39989 and :39989 hits are treat-as-malicious. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the IP/port at egress, capture the offending binary for hashing. 3) Hunt: extract the hard-coded IP/URL strings from the sample (Ghidra/strings), search the fleet for other hosts hitting the same D2IP endpoints with no preceding DNS, and feed confirmed IPs into the ZT-IP block-list.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteIP in ("154.92.19.71","2.26.98.67")
   or RemotePort == 39989
   or (isempty(RemoteUrl) and RemotePort > 1024
       and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","backgroundtransferhost.exe","onedrive.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","teams.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("154.92.19.71","2.26.98.67") or DstPortNumber == 39989
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

DeviceProcessEvents

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or SHA1 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or MD5 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or SHA1 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07") or MD5 in~ ("cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cc43cdbe8eb9874f55fffbe23b560b673eb9f31fb9a953926bba29464fd2dd07"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

How legitimate cloud platforms enable phishers to bypass MFA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-08-04 9 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

We cover a cloud-based AitM attack scenario leveraging service workers and Ultraviolet, and provide detailed phishing hosting statistics across platforms like Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, and IPFS.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] First-seen browser egress to abused cloud-PaaS phishing domains (workers.dev / pages.dev / vercel.app / github.io / netlify.app / dweb.link) · [LLM] Safe Links click resolving through a cloud-PaaS redirect chain into AitM phishing · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AitM session hijack: PaaS phishing-page visit followed by successful Entra sign-in from a different IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
First-seen browser egress to abused cloud-PaaS phishing domains (workers.dev / pages.dev / vercel.app / github.io / netlify.app / dweb.link) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a corporate browser making its first-ever connection (org-wide baseline anti-join) to a subdomain of the exact free-tier PaaS platforms this campaign abuses to host its AitM CAPTCHA relay and Ultraviolet reverse-proxy pages. Because the parent domains host millions of legit projects, the fidelity comes from the never-before-seen-in-org pivot, not the suffix alone. Rationale: Uses the exact PaaS suffix set from the article's statistics table (pages.dev 24.9%, vercel.app 13.8%, github.io 13.7%, netlify.app 10.0%, dweb.link 7.8%, plus workers.dev from the case study). Baseline anti-join is the noise reducer since these apex domains are shared with legit content. Cross-checked urlscan.io (Ultraviolet campaign) and RingSafe/Cofense Cloudflare-abuse reports. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://urlscan.io/blog/2026/04/15/ProxyingTrust/ • https://ringsafe.in/cloudflare-fronted-phishing-in-2026-how-workers-pages-tunnels-and-r2-became-default-phishing-infrastructure/ • https://cofense.com/blog/how-cloudflare-services-are-abused-for-credential-theft-and-malware-distribution
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.006 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/DevOps staff legitimately visiting a colleague's Cloudflare Pages or Vercel preview deployment
  • Open-source project documentation hosted on github.io
  • IPFS gateway (dweb.link) used by a legitimate web3/crypto app
  • Marketing landing pages a partner hosts on netlify.app
  • SaaS vendor status pages or serverless webhooks on workers.dev
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("devops-svc","builder")) and Devices == 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RemoteUrl/DstHostname and fetch it in a sandbox — a genuine hit shows a fake CAPTCHA gate or a Microsoft login iframe/BitB pop-up with a spoofed address bar. Check whether the same user received an inbound email whose link redirected here. 2) Contain: block the specific FQDN at proxy/DNS (not the apex), reset the user's Entra credentials and revoke all sessions/refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: search that user's SigninLogs for a successful MFA-satisfied sign-in from a datacenter/hosting IP within 30 min (AitM token replay) and check for new inbox rules or OAuth grants.

Safe Links click resolving through a cloud-PaaS redirect chain into AitM phishing AIDelivery Medium
Hunts UrlClickEvents where the resolved redirect chain (UrlChain) or final URL lands on one of the campaign's abused PaaS platforms — mirroring the article's Stage 1→2 flow of compromised-site CAPTCHA relay bouncing the victim to a *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy page. Targets the redirect landing, not the innocuous-looking link in the email body. Rationale: Anchors on the article's multi-stage redirect (email link -> compromised site CAPTCHA -> *.workers.dev), so it inspects the Safe Links UrlChain rather than the benign first-hop domain. ClickedThrough is the high-fidelity user-bypass signal. PaaS suffixes taken directly from the article's platform table. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://urlscan.io/blog/2026/04/15/ProxyingTrust/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1583.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit newsletter/marketing tracking link that happens to redirect through a Vercel/Netlify edge function
  • Internal app or CI notification linking to a github.io or pages.dev docs page
  • A vendor's URL-shortener whose final hop is a serverless health page
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platforms hosting lures on PaaS
  • Web3 wallet flows resolving through a dweb.link IPFS gateway
Suppression filter
| where IsClickedThrough == true or Workload == "Email"
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the full UrlChain terminal URL; confirm a Microsoft login iframe/BitB window and check whether the redirect emerged from a compromised legitimate first-hop domain. Confirm ActionType/IsClickedThrough (user actually reached the page). 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete the source message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents ZAP, block the terminal FQDN, force credential reset + session revocation for the clicker. 3) Hunt: enumerate other recipients of the same NetworkMessageId/sender, and pivot each clicker into UC-3 to catch AitM session replay.

UrlClickEvents

| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend Chain = tostring(UrlChain)

AitM session hijack: PaaS phishing-page visit followed by successful Entra sign-in from a different IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates an endpoint browser connecting to a campaign PaaS domain (Stage 2/3 Ultraviolet proxy + BitB) with a successful, MFA-satisfied Entra sign-in for the same user within 30 minutes whose source IP does NOT match the victim's device — the hallmark of the attacker replaying the intercepted session token from their own infrastructure. This is the payoff step the article describes: credentials and MFA relayed, then the attacker holds a live session. Rationale: Expresses the article's core AitM outcome: MFA relayed through the *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy, then the attacker uses the token from their own IP. The IP-mismatch clause (sign-in source != victim device public IP) within a 30-min window of the PaaS visit is the discriminator corroborated by Cofense/Securelist noting the token is replayed from a different IP/ASN than where the victim authenticated. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://cofense.com/blog/how-cloudflare-services-are-abused-for-credential-theft-and-malware-distribution • https://ringsafe.in/cloudflare-fronted-phishing-in-2026-how-workers-pages-tunnels-and-r2-became-default-phishing-infrastructure/
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1111 T1550.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User visits a legit PaaS-hosted app then signs in to M365 over corporate VPN/egress with a different public IP than the device reports
  • Roaming/mobile user whose device PublicIP and sign-in IP legitimately differ (cellular vs Wi-Fi)
  • CDN/proxy egress that rewrites the outbound IP for O365 traffic
  • Shared-device/kiosk scenarios where DeviceInfo PublicIP is stale
  • Developer testing their own Cloudflare Worker while authenticated to Azure
Suppression filter
| where SignInIP !in (dynamic([])) and Country != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sign-in IP is a hosting/datacenter ASN (not corporate egress or the user's ISP) and that the PaaS URL detonates to a Microsoft login/BitB page — that combination is a confirmed token theft. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens/sessions for the account (Entra 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-registration of MFA; block the SignInIP and PaaS FQDN. 3) Hunt: review AuditLogs/CloudAppEvents for attacker-created inbox forwarding rules, new OAuth app consents, MFA method additions, and mailbox exfiltration under that account after the sign-in time.
let Window = 30m;
let PhishConns = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
    | where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".pages.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".vercel.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".github.io" or RemoteUrl endswith ".netlify.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
    | project ConnTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, PhishUrl=RemoteUrl, UserUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn;
let DevIP = DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, PublicIP) by DeviceName;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SignInTime=Timestamp, AccountUpn, SignInIP=IPAddress, Application, Country, City
| join kind=inner PhishConns on $left.AccountUpn == $right.UserUpn
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| join kind=leftouter DevIP on DeviceName
| where isempty(PublicIP) or SignInIP != PublicIP
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), AccountUpn, DeviceName, PhishUrl, SignInIP, DevicePublicIP=PublicIP, Application, Country, City
| order by SignInTime desc
let Window = 30m;
let Phish = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstHostname endswith ".workers.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".pages.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".vercel.app" or DstHostname endswith ".github.io" or DstHostname endswith ".netlify.app" or DstHostname endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(SrcUsername)
    | project ConnTime=TimeGenerated, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, PhishHost=DstHostname;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| project SignInTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP=IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Location
| join kind=inner Phish on $left.UserPrincipalName == $right.SrcUsername
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| where SignInIP != SrcIpAddr
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), UserPrincipalName, PhishHost, SignInIP, VictimIP=SrcIpAddr, AppDisplayName, Location
| order by SignInTime desc
