Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

Sequelize Oracle SQLi: TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP quote-bypass payload in HTTP request AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP query strings / bodies carrying the CVE-2026-69240 payload shape — a parameter value beginning with TO_DATE( or TO_TIMESTAMP( followed by a quote break-out (||'', OR 1=1, --, UNION). This is the delivery vector that reaches Sequelize's vulnerable escape() path in the Oracle dialect. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC signature from the GHSA (`TO_DATE('0','Y')||'' OR 1=1--`): a param value opening with TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( plus a break-out token. Legitimate query params never combine an Oracle date-cast function with `||''`/`OR 1=1`/`--`, making this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/sequelize/CVE-2026-69240/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-SEQUELIZE-2959225 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DAST/pentest tooling (sqlmap, Burp Scanner, Acunetix) firing SQLi payloads during authorized testing
  • An internal application that legitimately accepts Oracle TO_DATE(...) expressions as a search parameter (rare)
  • Security awareness / red-team exercises replaying known CVE payloads
  • WAF that decodes and logs the raw attack even though it blocked the request (still a true attempt, triage as such)
  • Copy/paste of Oracle SQL snippets into a free-text search field by a developer
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("<known-scanner-ip-placeholder>") // replace/remove if no sanctioned scanners; prefer excluding by scanner UserAgent when available
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (SrcIP, UriPath, Query) and confirm the target app uses Sequelize with dialect=oracle and version < 6.37.4; check the HTTP status/response size to judge whether injection succeeded. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, add a virtual-patch rule dropping TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( in user input, and prioritise upgrading Sequelize to >= 6.37.4. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcIP for other endpoints/params hit, and cross-check the Oracle audit UC (below) for the same window to confirm the payload actually executed at the DB.
union
 (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=cIP, Host=Computer, Method=csMethod, UriPath=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, Status=tostring(scStatus)),
 (AppServiceHTTPLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=CIp, Host=CsHost, Method=CsMethod, UriPath=CsUriStem, Query=CsUriQuery, Status=tostring(ScStatus)),
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=SourceIP, Host=DestinationHostName, Method=RequestMethod, UriPath=RequestURL, Query=RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome))
| where Query has_any ("TO_DATE","TO_TIMESTAMP","to_date","to_timestamp")
| where Query matches regex @"(?i)(TO_DATE|TO_TIMESTAMP)\s*[\(%]"
| where Query has "||" or Query contains "%7C%7C" or Query matches regex @"(?i)\bor\b\s+1\s*=\s*1" or Query has "UNION" or Query contains "--"
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

DOUBLECUP ClickFix infrastructure: DNS/network to spoofed SaaS login IOC domains & IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts host resolution or connection to DOUBLECUP's known ClickFix delivery infrastructure — the fake NetSuite/Odoo/HubSpot login domains and the service's licensing/host IPs. Article-specific because it uses the exact IOCs SOCRadar tied to this campaign, not a generic phishing-domain heuristic. Rationale: Uses the exact SOCRadar-published IOC domains/IPs (login-netsuite.com, 213.139.77.109, 66.29.148.143). Cross-checked against the SOCRadar and The Hacker News write-ups of the same campaign — both list these SaaS-impersonation lures. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html

  • Threat-intel platform auto-enrichment resolving the IOC domains
  • A legitimately-registered lookalike domain later reclaimed by the impersonated vendor
  • URL-scanning proxy pre-fetching the domain on a user's behalf
  • Analyst manually browsing to the phishing page during triage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","smartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/user and the initiating process for the connection; confirm it was a user browser vs. a scanner/sandbox. 2) Contain: block the IOC domains/IPs at proxy/DNS/firewall and isolate the host if a non-browser process made the connection (indicates post-exec). 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to certutil/findstr browser-cache PNG extraction (UC2), RunMRU ClickFix artifacts (UC3), and outbound public-IP-check / blockchain-RPC calls (UC4/UC5).

Hunts the DOUBLECUP first-stage recovery step where a pasted command uses findstr or certutil to locate a PNG in the browser cache (by exact file size) and decode the hidden payload. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's quote: findstr/certutil 'searches the browser cache for the PNG based on its exact file size' to recover the hidden payload. certutil/findstr touching a browser cache PNG is near-zero in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe","msbuild.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"

1) Triage: pull the full command line and the parent process — a ClickFix chain shows explorer.exe/cmd.exe as parent and a specific byte-size filter. Recover the referenced PNG from cache for analysis. 2) Contain: isolate the host; kill the certutil/findstr and any child fileless second stage; capture memory. 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on public-IP lookup (UC4), blockchain-RPC C2 (UC5), CountLoader scheduled-task persistence, and DNS TXT tunneling (UC6) on the same host.

ClickFix clipboard-to-Run execution: RunMRU write + shell spawned from explorer AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the host-side artifact of DOUBLECUP's fake-CAPTCHA social engineering — the victim pasting the clipboard-staged command into the Win+R Run dialog. Detects the HKCU RunMRU value (and/or explorer spawning a shell) carrying the cache-search command. Article-specific: the copied command references certutil/findstr and the PNG cache. Rationale: The RunMRU key is the canonical forensic residue of the ClickFix 'paste into Run dialog' lure the article describes ('command automatically copied to their clipboard'). Constraining the value to certutil/findstr/.png/Cache ties it to this specific campaign rather than generic RunMRU noise. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/

Public-IPv4 discovery by non-browser process (environmental keying for payload decryption) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts DOUBLECUP's second-stage dropper retrieving the victim's public IPv4 to derive the SHA-256/CTR-XOR decryption key for the final payload. Detects a non-browser process resolving a public-IP-echo service — the environmental-keying tell that precedes in-memory execution. Article-specific per SOCRadar's IP-as-key analysis. Rationale: Encodes the article/SOCRadar detail that the dropper 'retrieves the victim's public IPv4 address and uses it to create a decryption key' via a SHA-256 CTR/XOR scheme. A non-browser process hitting an IP-echo service is the observable proxy for that keying step. DeviceManager EtherHiding: non-browser host querying Ethereum/Polygon RPC endpoints for C2 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts DeviceManager RAT resolving its live C2 IP from an Ethereum/Polygon smart contract (EtherHiding). Detects a non-developer/non-browser host reaching public blockchain RPC providers — a decentralized dead-drop resolver that resists takedown. Article-specific: SOCRadar attributes this exact EtherHiding C2-resolution behaviour to DeviceManager. Rationale: The article states DeviceManager 'uses a technique known as EtherHiding to retrieve its current C2 address from an Ethereum or Polygon smart contract.' A non-browser/non-dev process resolving public blockchain RPC providers is the network observable of that dead-drop resolver. Corroborated by SOCRadar and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html

DeviceManager DNS A/TXT tunneling for command retrieval and data exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts DeviceManager's DNS-based C2/exfil channel — using A and TXT records to pull commands, stage payloads, and beacon out stolen system data. Detects abnormal TXT-query volume per host and Python-driven DNS beaconing (DeviceManager is a Python RAT). Article-specific per SOCRadar's DNS A/TXT C2 analysis. Rationale: Encodes the article's statement that DeviceManager 'uses DNS A and TXT records to steal system information, retrieve commands to execute, download payloads, and send command output.' High per-host TXT volume + Python-driven DNS beaconing are the two orthogonal observables of that channel. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Email-security gateways doing bulk SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT lookups
  • Certificate automation (ACME/DNS-01) issuing TXT queries
  • Python monitoring scripts performing frequent DNS lookups
  • Security scanners enumerating TXT records
  • Service-discovery tools polling DNS-SD TXT records
Suppression filter
| where not (SampleName has_any ("_dmarc","_domainkey","_acme-challenge","spf"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the queried domains and TXT payloads for base64/hex-encoded blobs and abnormally long labels; benign TXT (SPF/DMARC/ACME) is short and to well-known apex domains. Confirm the initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the tunneling domain/resolver, and preserve the Python process/memory. 3) Hunt: pivot to the EtherHiding C2 resolution (UC5), the IPv4-keyed decrypt (UC4), and the original ClickFix delivery domain (UC1) to scope the full chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| summarize DnsConnCount = count(), DistinctResolvers = dcount(RemoteIP), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DnsConnCount > 100  // 100 = well above benign python DNS/day; DeviceManager beacons far more
| order by DnsConnCount desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where QueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize TxtQueryCount = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(Name), SampleName = any(Name), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, ClientIP
| where TxtQueryCount > 50  // 50 = P99 TXT lookups/host/day; benign hosts issue <10
| order by TxtQueryCount desc

CountLoader macOS LaunchAgent recon: sw_vers/system_profiler/ioreg clustered under one parent AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the macOS CountLoader variant that fingerprints the host with built-in utilities (sw_vers, system_profiler, ioreg, curl) before installing a LaunchAgent for persistence. Detects three-or-more of these recon binaries spawned by one non-interactive parent. Article-specific: SOCRadar names this exact utility set for the Intel/Apple-Silicon CountLoader build. Rationale: Directly uses the article's named macOS recon set ('built-in utilities such as curl, sw_vers, system_profiler, and ioreg') plus LaunchAgent persistence. Clustering ≥3 of these under one non-shell parent distinguishes malware fingerprinting from an admin typing them interactively. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1082 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDM/RMM inventory agents (Jamf, Kandji) enumerating hardware
  • Legitimate installers running system_profiler for compatibility checks
  • IT diagnostic scripts run over SSH
  • Asset-management tooling collecting ioreg/sw_vers output
  • Developer build scripts probing the host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/Library/Application Support/JAMF" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jamf","kandji-daemon","osqueryd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and whether it is signed/notarized; a curl call to an unknown host immediately after the recon cluster is the malicious tell. Check ~/Library/LaunchAgents for a new plist. 2) Contain: isolate the Mac, remove the malicious LaunchAgent plist, and kill the parent process. 3) Hunt: review outbound curl destinations for C2, and check for the CountLoader Windows path (scheduled tasks, browser-wallet/extension enumeration) across the fleet. Sentinel/Datadog left empty — this tenant has no macOS EDR table equivalent to MDE DeviceProcessEvents.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("sw_vers","system_profiler","ioreg","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("bash","zsh","sh","Terminal","login")
| summarize Utils = make_set(FileName), SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where array_length(set_intersect(Utils, dynamic(["sw_vers","system_profiler","ioreg"]))) >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("sw_vers","system_profiler","ioreg","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("bash","zsh","sh","Terminal","login")
| summarize Utils = make_set(FileName), SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where array_length(set_intersect(Utils, dynamic(["sw_vers","system_profiler","ioreg"]))) >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(sw_vers|system_profiler|ioreg|curl)$/i
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/^(bash|zsh|sh|Terminal|login)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctUtils))
| DistinctUtils >= 3
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` values(Processes.process_name) as procs values(Processes.process) as cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("sw_vers","system_profiler","ioreg","curl")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search procs="system_profiler" procs="ioreg" procs="sw_vers"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false values(Processes.process_name) as procs values(Processes.process) as cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("sw_vers","system_profiler","ioreg","curl")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake Xeno Executor installers are infecting unsuspecting Roblox players with malware that provides remote access and steals sensitive information. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Roblox Xeno script launcher pushes infostealer, RAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Fake Xeno loader (xeno.exe) executed from archive/Downloads or Xeno cache path · [LLM] Java runtime (javaw.exe) extracted to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java by fake Xeno loader · [LLM] decompiler.exe (masqueraded Java JAR) spawned by javaw.exe / xeno.exe · [LLM] 'Display Calibration' Run key persistence pointing to LocalAppData Java/GameDVR payload
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Fake Xeno C2 beacon to solthere.net / LocalAppData javaw.exe public egress · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Single non-browser process reads credential stores across 3+ browsers (Chrome/Edge/Brave/Opera/Vivaldi) · [LLM] Exodus wallet tamper (app.asar) / multi-wallet enumeration by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Fake Xeno loader (xeno.exe) executed from archive/Downloads or Xeno cache path AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of a binary named xeno.exe from user-writable extraction paths (%TEMP%, Downloads, %APPDATA%, or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Xeno\workspace\cache) — the first-stage loader of the fake Xeno Roblox executor campaign. Legitimate Xeno is a fringe third-party tool and this specific cache/temp launch pattern with an archive-tool parent is high fidelity for the malicious repackage. Rationale: Uses the exact loader name xeno.exe plus the Bitdefender-confirmed staging path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Xeno\workspace\cache and the article's ZIP/self-extract delivery to user-writable dirs; the name+path combination is specific to this repackage rather than generic User Execution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.threatlocker.com/blog/powercat-malware-campaign-fake-game-cheats-deliver-infostealer-targeting-discord-roblox-and-crypto-wallets
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A player legitimately runs the real Xeno executor after unzipping it to Downloads (real Xeno is itself an unsanctioned tool, so treat as policy hit)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox under a user profile
  • Portable-app launchers that stage tools to %TEMP% and happen to include an unrelated xeno.exe
  • Backup/AV software briefly copying the archive into a Temp scan folder before launch
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","7zfm.exe","7zg.exe","explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","WinRAR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and check against the Bitdefender MD5 list; confirm parent is an archive tool (winrar/7zip/explorer SFX) and folder is user-writable. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the xeno.exe process tree, and block the hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for javaw.exe extracted to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java, a decompiler.exe child, the 'Display Calibration' Run key, and outbound traffic to solthere.net.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "xeno.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\Xeno\workspace\cache\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\xeno.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\Xeno\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fake Xeno Roblox Loader Execution from User-Writable Path
id: 6f3b2c1a-9d84-4a7e-b0c2-7e5f1a9c3d21
description: Detects xeno.exe (fake Xeno Roblox executor first-stage loader) executing from Temp, Downloads, Roaming or the Xeno workspace cache path.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/
  - https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\xeno.exe'
    Image|contains:
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\'
      - '\AppData\Local\Xeno\workspace\cache\'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\Temp\*\xeno.exe OR *\Downloads\*\xeno.exe OR *\Roaming\*\xeno.exe OR *\Xeno\workspace\cache\xeno.exe OR *\Temp\*\Xeno.exe OR *\Downloads\*\XENO.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\xeno\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\(Temp|Downloads|Roaming|cache)\\\\", field=ImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="xeno.exe" (Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Xeno\\workspace\\cache\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="xeno.exe" (Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Xeno\\workspace\\cache\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Java runtime (javaw.exe) extracted to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java by fake Xeno loader AIInstallation High
Hunts the fake Xeno loader self-provisioning a private JRE — javaw.exe/java.exe written into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin by a non-installer process (typically xeno.exe). The article states the payload 'checks for a Java Runtime Environment and extracts one if necessary'; Bitdefender confirms the exact drop path, making this a strong pre-execution marker of the multi-stage chain. Rationale: Anchors on Bitdefender's confirmed drop path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe combined with the article's 'extracts a JRE if necessary' behavior; a private JRE written into LocalAppData by a non-installer is abnormal and specific to this loader's setup phase. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer unzipping a portable JDK/JRE into a user profile for local builds
  • Minecraft/modded-launcher installers bundling their own JRE under AppData
  • Enterprise app repackaging that stages a private Java runtime per-user
  • CI/build agents extracting Java toolchains to a workspace under LocalAppData
Suppression filter
| where DropperPath !has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\" and Dropper !in~ ("MinecraftInstaller.exe","MinecraftLauncher.exe","prismlauncher.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the dropper process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — if it is xeno.exe or an unsigned binary from Temp/Downloads, escalate. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the dropped javaw.exe and the parent loader, block the loader hash. 3) Hunt: pivot to any javaw.exe execution from this path spawning decompiler.exe, plus GameDVR payload dir and solthere.net C2 on the same device.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("javaw.exe", "java.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Java\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "setup.exe", "jre-installer.exe", "java_installer.exe", "jdk-installer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          Dropper = InitiatingProcessFileName, DropperPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          DropperCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("javaw.exe", "java.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Local\Java\"
| where ActingProcessName !has "installer" and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\msiexec.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JRE javaw.exe Dropped to LocalAppData by Non-Installer
id: b2a7d519-4c60-4f3b-9a1e-2c8f0d6e4b77

decompiler.exe (masqueraded Java JAR) spawned by javaw.exe / xeno.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the second-stage of the fake Xeno chain: an obfuscated Java payload disguised as decompiler.exe launched by javaw.exe (or directly by xeno.exe) from a user AppData path. The article explicitly names this file and its environment-check / victim-registration role; the javaw→decompiler.exe parentage is anomalous and campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly named decompiler.exe (an obfuscated Java payload) with the Bitdefender-confirmed javaw.exe parentage; a Java runtime spawning a binary named after a decompiler tool from LocalAppData is a precise masquerading IOC unique to this chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A reverse-engineer legitimately running a Java decompiler GUI packaged as decompiler.exe
  • IDE/dev tooling that wraps a decompiler and is launched via javaw
  • Security lab detonation of the sample
  • Renamed legitimate decompiler utilities placed in a user profile by a developer
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java and the file hash matches the Bitdefender Stage-2 MD5 (d123dbb5c5980bfeb22586197d2cc403); check for outbound registration traffic right after. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the javaw/decompiler tree, block hashes. 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on GameDVR javaw.exe process, browser credential-store access, and the 'Display Calibration' persistence key.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "decompiler.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("javaw.exe", "java.exe", "xeno.exe")
     or FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"

          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Single non-browser process reads credential stores across 3+ browsers (Chrome/Edge/Brave/Opera/Vivaldi) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the stealer stage: one process opening Login Data / Cookies / Web Data / Local State across three or more of the five browsers the malware targets within one activity window. The article's explicit browser list (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi) plus a non-browser reader makes rapid multi-browser fan-out a high-fidelity credential-theft signal. Rationale: Uses the article's exact five-browser target list and Chromium credential-store filenames; requiring a single non-browser process to fan out across >=3 browsers in one window filters normal browser self-access and yields the stealer's harvesting behavior. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, Dashlane) importing saved logins from multiple installed browsers
  • Enterprise browser-migration or profile-backup tooling reading Login Data across browsers
  • EDR/AV modules scanning browser credential files
  • A sync/backup agent (OneDrive/roaming profiles) copying browser profile folders
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("1password.exe","bitwarden.exe","dashlane.exe","keeperpasswordmanager.exe","opera_autoupdate.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the reading process — if it is javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA% or an unsigned binary, treat as confirmed stealer; note which browsers were touched. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, force-reset passwords and revoke sessions for the affected user (browser-saved creds are assumed compromised). 3) Hunt: check for Discord/Roblox/Minecraft token access, Exodus wallet reads, and outbound C2 to solthere.net from the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data", "Cookies", "Web Data", "Local State")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", "BraveSoftware", "Opera Software", @"\Vivaldi\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","vivaldi.exe","explorer.exe","onedrive.exe")
| extend Browser = case(
    FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\", "Chrome",
    FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\Edge\", "Edge",
    FolderPath has "BraveSoftware", "Brave",
    FolderPath has "Opera Software", "Opera",
    FolderPath has @"\Vivaldi\", "Vivaldi", "Other")
| summarize BrowserCount = dcount(Browser), Browsers = make_set(Browser),
            StoreSamples = make_set(FolderPath, 10), StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where BrowserCount >= 3   // one non-browser process touching >=3 of the 5 targeted browsers
| order by BrowserCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data", "Cookies", "Web Data", "Local State")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", "BraveSoftware", "Opera Software", @"\Vivaldi\")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","explorer.exe","onedrive.exe"))
| extend Browser = case(
    TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\", "Chrome",
    TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\Edge\", "Edge",
    TargetFilePath has "BraveSoftware", "Brave",
    TargetFilePath has "Opera Software", "Opera",
    TargetFilePath has @"\Vivaldi\", "Vivaldi", "Other")
| summarize BrowserCount = dcount(Browser), Browsers = make_set(Browser), StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActorUsername
| where BrowserCount >= 3
| order by BrowserCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\Google\Chrome\* OR *\Microsoft\Edge\* OR *\BraveSoftware\* OR *\Opera Software\* OR *\Vivaldi\*) @TargetFilename:(*Login Data* OR *Cookies* OR *Web Data* OR *Local State*) -@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\opera.exe OR *\vivaldi.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/\\(Google\\Chrome|Microsoft\\Edge|BraveSoftware|Opera Software|Vivaldi)\\.*(Login Data|Cookies|Web Data|Local State)$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|opera|vivaldi|explorer)\.exe$/i
| Browser := if(regex("Google\\\\Chrome", field=TargetFileName), then="Chrome", else=if(regex("Microsoft\\\\Edge", field=TargetFileName), then="Edge", else=if(regex("BraveSoftware", field=TargetFileName), then="Brave", else=if(regex("Opera", field=TargetFileName), then="Opera", else="Vivaldi"))))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(Browser, distinct=true, as=BrowserCount), collect([Browser])])
| BrowserCount >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Local State") (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Edge\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\BraveSoftware\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Opera Software\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Vivaldi\\*") Filesystem.process_name!="chrome.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="msedge.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="brave.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="opera.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="vivaldi.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id | eval browsers=mvdedup(mvmap(paths, case(like(paths,"%Google\Chrome%"),"Chrome", like(paths,"%Microsoft\Edge%"),"Edge", like(paths,"%BraveSoftware%"),"Brave", like(paths,"%Opera Software%"),"Opera", like(paths,"%Vivaldi%"),"Vivaldi"))) | eval browser_count=mvcount(browsers) | where browser_count>=3 | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Local State") (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Edge\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\BraveSoftware\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Opera Software\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Vivaldi\\*") Filesystem.process_name!="chrome.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="msedge.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="brave.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="opera.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="vivaldi.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id | eval browsers=mvdedup(mvmap(paths, case(like(paths,"%Google\Chrome%"),"Chrome", like(paths,"%Microsoft\Edge%"),"Edge", like(paths,"%BraveSoftware%"),"Brave", like(paths,"%Opera Software%"),"Opera", like(paths,"%Vivaldi%"),"Vivaldi"))) | eval browser_count=mvcount(browsers) | where browser_count>=3 | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Exodus wallet tamper (app.asar) / multi-wallet enumeration by non-wallet process AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the crypto-theft stage: a non-wallet process writing to the Exodus app.asar (the malware's app.asar injection technique) or reading across multiple wallet directories. The article calls out dedicated Exodus targeting; Bitdefender confirms app.asar injection against Exodus 26.1.5, making an unexpected app.asar write the crown-jewel IOC. Rationale: Anchors on the article's dedicated Exodus targeting plus Bitdefender's confirmed app.asar-injection detail; an app.asar write from anything other than Exodus/Update is a precise wallet-backdoor IOC, with multi-wallet-dir fan-out as a secondary enumeration signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1005 T1518 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Exodus auto-update rewriting app.asar (usually via Update.exe/electron)
  • A backup tool copying the whole wallet directory tree
  • Antivirus scanning wallet folders and touching app.asar
  • User manually reinstalling/repairing an Electron wallet app
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("exodus update.exe","squirrel.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\AppData\Local\exodus\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process is not Exodus's own updater — if it is javaw.exe or an unsigned binary, treat the wallet as backdoored. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and advise the user to move funds from a clean device and rotate seed phrases immediately. 3) Hunt: correlate with browser credential theft, Discord/Roblox token access, and C2 to solthere.net on the same host and user.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has @"\Exodus\")
     or FolderPath has_any (@"\Exodus\exodus.wallet\", @"\Electrum\wallets\", @"\Ledger Live\", @"\atomic\Local Storage\", @"\Coinomi\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("exodus.exe", "electrum.exe", "ledger live.exe", "atomic.exe", "update.exe", "electron.exe")
| summarize WalletHits = count(), Ops = make_set(ActionType), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 15),
            AsarWrite = countif(FileName =~ "app.asar" and ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")),
            StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where AsarWrite > 0 or WalletHits >= 2
| order by AsarWrite desc, WalletHits desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "app.asar" and TargetFilePath has @"\Exodus\")
     or TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Exodus\exodus.wallet\", @"\Electrum\wallets\", @"\Ledger Live\", @"\atomic\Local Storage\", @"\Coinomi\")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("exodus.exe","electrum.exe","atomic.exe","update.exe","electron.exe"))
| summarize WalletHits = count(), Ops = make_set(DvcAction), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 15),
            AsarWrite = countif(TargetFileName =~ "app.asar"),
            StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActorUsername
| where AsarWrite > 0 or WalletHits >= 2
| order by AsarWrite desc

'Display Calibration' Run key persistence pointing to LocalAppData Java/GameDVR payload AIInstallation High
Hunts the fake Xeno persistence: a HKCU Run value named 'Display Calibration' (Bitdefender-confirmed) and/or any Run value whose data points at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR javaw.exe. This masquerading autostart name is specific to the campaign and gives a durable install-phase pivot. Rationale: Combines Bitdefender's confirmed 'Display Calibration' Run-value name with the confirmed payload dirs (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Java, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR) so the rule fires on both the named value and any Run entry launching the javaw payload — both campaign-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine display-calibration utility that legitimately registers a Run key (rare; verify the data path)
  • Admin scripts adding Run entries that reference AppData for other apps
  • Software installers that place a per-user javaw autostart for a benign Java app
  • Roaming-profile replication re-writing existing Run values
Suppression filter
| where WriterPath has @"\AppData\Local\" or Writer in~ ("javaw.exe","xeno.exe","decompiler.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the RegistryValueData — if it launches javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java or GameDVR, it is confirmed malicious. 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the Run value and the StartupApproved\Run entry, quarantine the GameDVR payload dir, and kill any live javaw.exe from those paths. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same 'Display Calibration' value name and the GameDVR javaw process, then pivot to C2 solthere.net.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Display Calibration"
     or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Java\", @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR", "javaw.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName, WriterPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Display Calibration"
     or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Java\", @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR", "javaw.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake Xeno C2 beacon to solthere.net / LocalAppData javaw.exe public egress AICommand & Control High
Hunts command-and-control for the campaign: DNS/HTTPS to solthere.net (victim registration /justacoolkat10 and payload /api/v1/redeem) or a javaw.exe running from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR making public outbound connections. Combines a confirmed C2 domain with the payload's abnormal egress process/path. Rationale: Ships the Bitdefender-confirmed C2 domain solthere.net (with the /justacoolkat10 and /api/v1/redeem endpoints) and pairs it with the abnormal behavioral egress of javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java or GameDVR so the rule still fires if infrastructure rotates. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate in-AppData Java apps (e.g. some Minecraft launchers place javaw under AppData) making internet calls — verify domain
  • Threat-intel or sandbox appliance resolving solthere.net for research
  • Proxy/secure-web-gateway pre-fetching or sinkholing the domain
  • A benign Java tool updated into GameDVR by unrelated software
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\.minecraft\") and RemoteUrl !has "solthere.net")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving/connecting process is javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java or GameDVR and check for the preceding xeno.exe/decompiler.exe chain. 2) Contain: isolate host, block solthere.net and the dynamic .xyz C2 at the proxy/firewall, kill the javaw process, quarantine the GameDVR payload. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy logs fleet-wide for solthere.net, then correlate hosts with the 'Display Calibration' Run key and browser/wallet theft.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "solthere.net"
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "javaw.exe"
         and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Java\", @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\GameDVR")
         and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has "solthere.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Domain = Name, Source = "DNS"),
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Url has "solthere.net" or DstHostname has "solthere.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DstHostname, Source = "NetSession")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

18 Malicious npm Packages Deliver Cross-Platform RAT to Alibaba Tool Users

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 15 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new set of malicious npm packages that target users of Alibaba developer tools with a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT) as part of a sophisticated, targeted software supply chain attack targeting Chinese-speaking environments. One of the packages in question is "lib-mtop," an unscoped package with the same name as a private Alibaba package

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious @ali-impersonating npm packages installed into node_modules (Alibaba RAT cluster) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm/node loader spawning curl to fetch remote JavaScript from decoy Alibaba domains · [LLM] Linux RAT payload dropped to /tmp then self-deleted after in-memory load · [LLM] macOS RAT persistence via ~/.zshrc injection and 10-minute LaunchAgent · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network callback to decoy Alibaba OSS / Aliyun Function Compute RAT C2 hosts · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] mrmustard PyPI stealer exfil to metrics.femboy.energy / webhook.site · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Malicious @ali-impersonating npm packages installed into node_modules (Alibaba RAT cluster) AIDelivery High
Detects installation of the 18 named npm packages from the Socket-reported cross-platform RAT campaign that impersonate private @ali-scoped Alibaba packages. Fires on file writes into node_modules for any of the exact malicious package names, which is the earliest on-host signal of dependency-tree compromise. Rationale: Uses the complete verbatim package list from the article/Socket disclosure scoped to node_modules paths, so any hit is one of the exact malicious artifacts, not a generic supply-chain heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://cybersecuritynews.com/npm-packages-cross-platform-rat/ • https://gbhackers.com/split-rat-components-across-npm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named an internal package identically (e.g. a real private local-config-parser mirrored offline)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the packages in a sandbox
  • Package cache/mirror sync (Verdaccio/Nexus) replicating the names before removal
  • Old lockfile restore pulling a pre-March 2026 benign lib-mtop version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm which package + version installed and whether the host has access to the real @ali-scoped registry (the campaign only fully activates in Alibaba-adjacent environments). Check the package.json dependency tree for smart-config-manager as the bridge. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the developer host, kill node processes, remove node_modules, and treat the machine as compromised. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same DeviceName for curl-fetched JS and the decoy aliyuncs/fcapp C2 callbacks; rotate any credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens present on the host from a clean machine.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

npm/node loader spawning curl to fetch remote JavaScript from decoy Alibaba domains AIInstallation High
Detects the lib-mtop loader behaviour where a Node/npm process shells out to curl to download a hardcoded remote JavaScript payload that is then executed via require(). Scopes to curl children of node/npm whose command line references the campaign's aliyuncs/fcapp/ai-app.pub decoy hosts. Rationale: Pairs the article's stated loader mechanic (node -> curl -> require) with the specific C2 host substrings, giving a parent-child + command-line triple that no legitimate npm workflow produces. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://cybersecuritynews.com/npm-packages-cross-platform-rat/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build script legitimately using curl to pull a tarball from a real aliyuncs.com OSS bucket (verify exact subdomain against IOC list)
  • Node-based CI tooling that fetches assets via curl during install
  • Developer manually testing curl from an npm run-script
  • Internal package that vendors curl-based postinstall fetch of internal artifacts
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the full curl URL from the command line and compare the host against the IOC set (aone-cli-next.oss-cn-beijing.aliyuncs.com and siblings); benign OSS buckets differ in subdomain. Step 2 (contain): Kill the node and curl processes, block the resolved host at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the downloaded JS being require()'d, any vm-module secondary payload, and follow-on OS-specific persistence (UC4/UC5) on the same DeviceName.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aliyuncs.com","fcapp.run","ai-app.pub")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("aliyuncs.com","fcapp.run","ai-app.pub")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network callback to decoy Alibaba OSS / Aliyun Function Compute RAT C2 hosts AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS/network egress to the campaign's payload-staging and C2 domains that masquerade as Alibaba OSS and Aliyun Function Compute endpoints to blend into legitimate Alibaba traffic. These full hostnames are hard IOCs from the article's pre-extracted set. Rationale: These are fully-qualified IOC hostnames unique to the campaign; the aone-* aliyuncs subdomains are attacker-controlled buckets distinct from generic *.aliyuncs.com, so exact-match keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://gbhackers.com/split-rat-components-across-npm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or IOC-validation tooling resolving the hosts on purpose
  • Proxy/DNS security appliance pre-resolving submitted URLs for categorization
  • An analyst manually curling the IOC during investigation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (node/curl vs browser) and whether the resolution succeeded and returned data. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block the domains org-wide, isolate the resolving host, and snapshot for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with UC1/UC2 on the same host, review outbound bytes to the resolved IP for secondary-payload download, and sweep all dev hosts' DNS logs for the same five hosts.

Linux RAT payload dropped to /tmp then self-deleted after in-memory load AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Linux branch of the RAT that downloads a binary to /tmp, runs it as a detached process, and deletes the file from disk once loaded into memory. Correlates a short-lived /tmp file create+delete pair on the same host driven by a download/interpreter process. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact Linux TTP (download to /tmp, detached exec, delete-after-load) as a create+delete correlation restricted to download/interpreter processes, which is the defining anti-forensic behaviour of this branch. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package managers extracting to /tmp and cleaning up (apt, pip build temp dirs)
  • Shell scripts using mktemp for transient work files
  • Compilers/CI writing and removing intermediate objects in /tmp
  • Browser or updater temp-download-then-move operations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("mktemp","apt","dpkg","pip"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Recover the initiating command line and the /tmp filename; check whether the detached process is still resident (ps/lsof by inode) despite the on-disk file being gone. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, capture memory of the orphaned/detached process before reboot, and block associated C2. Step 3 (hunt): Tie back to UC1/UC3 for the npm install and aliyuncs download that seeded it, and check for lateral-movement attempts described as a final-payload capability.
let Created = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","node","bash","sh")
| project CreateTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| project DeleteTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath
| join kind=inner Created on DeviceName, FolderPath
| where DeleteTime between (CreateTime .. CreateTime + 5m)
| project DeviceName, FolderPath, CreateTime, DeleteTime, SecondsAlive=datetime_diff('second', DeleteTime, CreateTime), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by CreateTime desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileDeleted")
| summarize Events=make_set(EventType), CreateTime=minif(TimeGenerated, EventType=="FileCreated"), DeleteTime=maxif(TimeGenerated, EventType=="FileDeleted"), Proc=any(ActingProcessName) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath
| where array_length(Events)==2 and DeleteTime > CreateTime and datetime_diff('minute', DeleteTime, CreateTime) <= 5
| where Proc has_any ("curl","wget","node","bash","sh")
| order by CreateTime desc
source:linux.auditd @process.name:(curl OR wget OR node) @process.command_line:(*\/tmp\/*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^\/tmp\// ContextImageFileName=/(curl|wget|node|bash|sh)$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=FileDeleted TargetFileName=/^\/tmp\//}, field=[aid, TargetFileName], include=[TargetFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false values(Filesystem.action) as actions min(_time) as create_time max(_time) as delete_time count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/*" (Filesystem.action=created OR Filesystem.action=deleted) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where mvcount(actions)=2 AND (delete_time - create_time) <= 300 | sort - create_time
macOS RAT persistence via ~/.zshrc injection and 10-minute LaunchAgent AIInstallation Medium
Detects the macOS branch of the RAT that persists by inserting a background script into ~/.zshrc and installing a LaunchAgent plist. Scopes file writes to those two persistence locations when driven by node/npm/curl/osascript rather than an interactive shell editor. Rationale: Combines the two named macOS persistence locations from the article with a non-interactive writer constraint (node/npm/curl/osascript), which cleanly separates the malware's scripted write from a developer editing their own shell profile. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba
ATT&CKT1546.004 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dotfile managers (chezmoi, yadm) or Homebrew post-install writing to .zshrc
  • Legitimate app installers dropping their own LaunchAgent plist
  • Developer tooling (nvm, pyenv) appending shell-init lines to .zshrc
  • IDE/setup scripts registering a LaunchAgent for background services
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chezmoi","yadm","brew","nvm","pyenv"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the injected .zshrc line / LaunchAgent plist ProgramArguments and check the referenced binary or URL against the campaign IOCs (aliyuncs/fcapp hosts). Note the LaunchAgent's 10-minute StartInterval as a strong tell. Step 2 (contain): Remove the persistence entries, unload the LaunchAgent, isolate the host, kill resident RAT processes. Step 3 (hunt): Check for injection into DingTalk/Wukong/Qoder collaboration apps, correlate to UC1's npm install, and rotate developer credentials from a clean machine.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","curl","osascript")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","curl","osascript")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mrmustard PyPI stealer exfil to metrics.femboy.energy / webhook.site AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the secondary campaign in the article: the trojanized mrmustard 0.7.4 PyPI package whose _check_tf_compatibility() stealer harvests SSH keys, AWS creds and Kubernetes configs and beacons to metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect (XOR key tf_compat_v2), with CI publishing-secret exfil to a webhook.site URL. Fires on egress to those hosts. Rationale: metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect is the confirmed C2 (StepSecurity/SafeDep, decoded from XOR key tf_compat_v2) and the webhook.site GUID is the exact CI-secret exfil sink named in the article; both are hard IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-pypi-mrmustard-0-7-4-credential-stealer • https://safedep.io/mrmustard-malicious-pypi-package/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using webhook.site for their own webhook testing (validate the exact GUID path)
  • Security research/detonation of mrmustard in a sandbox
  • IOC-validation curling the C2
  • webhook.site used by an unrelated internal integration test
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (python importing mrmustard is the tell) and whether the destination is the exact webhook.site GUID vs generic testing. Confirm mrmustard 0.7.4 is installed (pip show). Step 2 (contain): Block femboy.energy and the webhook.site URL, isolate the host, and immediately treat SSH keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configs, and any CI publishing tokens on that host as compromised — rotate from a clean machine. Step 3 (hunt): Remove the three persistence mechanisms that survive uninstall, downgrade mrmustard, and audit CI runners for the self-hosted-runner probing / secret theft described in the report.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("metrics.femboy.energy","webhook.site/710babde-6ace-47fe-83f4-9688e6548df9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "femboy.energy" or DnsQuery == "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
