Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inside the Underground Business of the Android BTMOB RAT malware

BleepingComputer
2026-08-03 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Flare researchers analyzed thousands of underground posts to examine how the BTMOB Android malware operation evolved into a fragmented ecosystem of resellers, source-code vendors, custom versions, and competing sales channels. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] BTMOB RAT APK sample hash observed on managed endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Inside the Underground Business of the Android BTMOB RAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to server.yaarsa.com / 78.135.93.123 · [LLM] BTMOB RAT C2 URI path /yaarsa/private/ and WebSocket /con endpoint
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to server.yaarsa.com / 78.135.93.123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections and DNS resolutions from any monitored endpoint (including Defender/Falcon mobile agents and corporate proxy/firewall) to the confirmed BTMOB RAT C2 infrastructure. High-fidelity because the IP and WebSocket C2 domain are corroborated by Palo Alto Unit42 and Cyble as dedicated BTMOB operator infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the confirmed C2 IP 78.135.93.123 and WebSocket C2 domain server.yaarsa.com; both appear in Palo Alto Unit42's BTMOB IOC list and Cyble's analysis (hxxp://78.135.93.123/yaarsa/private/ and hxxp://server.yaarsa.com/con), making them dedicated-infrastructure indicators rather than shared hosting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/PaloAltoNetworks/Unit42-timely-threat-intel/blob/main/2025-05-21-IOCs-for-BTMOB-RAT-activity.txt • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://any.run/malware-trends/btmob/
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sandbox or MTD detonation lab intentionally resolving/connecting to server.yaarsa.com
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling proactively resolving the C2 domain from a SOC workstation
  • IP 78.135.93.123 later reassigned by the hosting provider to a benign tenant
  • Security crawler or blocklist-feed validator probing the domain
  • Analyst manually browsing the C2 URL during triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating device and process; if it is a corporate mobile/MDM-managed device, treat as likely compromised — confirm it is not a sandbox/scanner asset. 2) Contain: block 78.135.93.123 and server.yaarsa.com at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the device, and force credential resets for accounts used on that phone (BTMOB harvests logins via Accessibility overlays). 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for the BTMOB APK hashes (see companion UC), check for other endpoints resolving server.yaarsa.com or the extended Unit42 C2 IP set, and review authentication logs for logins sourced from the infected device post-infection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "78.135.93.123" or RemoteUrl has "server.yaarsa.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP == "78.135.93.123" or DestinationHostName has "server.yaarsa.com" or RequestURL has "server.yaarsa.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, Activity ),
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "server.yaarsa.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResolvedIP = Result )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BTMOB RAT C2 URI path /yaarsa/private/ and WebSocket /con endpoint AICommand & Control High
Hunts web-proxy/URL telemetry for the distinctive BTMOB C2 request patterns: the PHP handler path /yaarsa/private/ and the server.yaarsa.com/con WebSocket endpoint. Distinct from the IP/DNS pivot because it survives C2 IP rotation and catches the exact application-layer request shape documented by Cyble. Rationale: Uses Cyble's documented BTMOB C2 application-layer artefacts: the PHP handler path hxxp://78.135.93.123/yaarsa/private/yarsap_80541.php and the WebSocket endpoint hxxp://server.yaarsa.com/con carrying the 'BTMOB'/'BT-v' handshake — path strings that are unique to this RAT family. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because their standard telemetry (Sysmon EID3, FDR NetworkConnect, CloudTrail) does not carry full request URIs. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://any.run/malware-trends/btmob/
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1521
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Proxy content-inspection appliance replaying/sanitising the captured URL
  • Security web crawler or URL sandbox fetching the C2 path during analysis
  • Analyst manually retrieving the C2 URI while investigating a sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host and whether the request succeeded (HTTP 101/200 to /con indicates an established WebSocket beacon = active compromise, not a one-off probe). 2) Contain: block server.yaarsa.com and the URI patterns at the proxy, isolate the source device, and revoke sessions/credentials entered on it. 3) Hunt: sweep proxy logs for any host hitting /yaarsa/private/ or */con on BTMOB C2 hosts, and correlate with the BTMOB APK-hash file detection to confirm the implant on the device.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/yaarsa/private/" or (RemoteUrl has "server.yaarsa.com" and RemoteUrl has "/con")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where RequestURL has "/yaarsa/private/" or RequestURL has "server.yaarsa.com/con"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication ),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has "/yaarsa/private/" or Url has "server.yaarsa.com/con"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname = HttpHostName, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BTMOB RAT APK sample hash observed on managed endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts file telemetry for known BTMOB RAT APK sample hashes landing on any Defender/Sentinel-monitored device — including Defender for Endpoint on Android, MDM-synced stores, or a Windows host used to stage/distribute the dropper. Article-specific because it matches the exact BTMOB sample SHA256 set, one of which is corroborated in the Unit42 IOC bundle. Rationale: Matches the exact BTMOB APK SHA256 sample set from the article's IOC bundle; hash 8dbfcf6b67ee6c5821564bf4228099beaf5f40e4a87118cbb1e52d8f01312f40 is independently confirmed in Palo Alto Unit42's BTMOB IOC list, validating the family attribution. Datadog/Falcon/Sigma left empty because their standard file telemetry (Sysmon FileCreate, FDR FileWritten) does not carry SHA256 on file-write events. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/PaloAltoNetworks/Unit42-timely-threat-intel/blob/main/2025-05-21-IOCs-for-BTMOB-RAT-activity.txt • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender AV writing the sample into its quarantine folder (MsMpEng.exe / MsSense.exe)
  • Malware analyst downloading the APK into a sandbox or research VM
  • Threat-intel repository/sample-feed sync populating a hash store on a SOC host
  • EDR telemetry from an intentionally-infected test device in a mobile security lab
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe") and FolderPath !contains "Windows Defender\\Quarantine"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device is a real user/mobile asset (not a sandbox/quarantine event) and identify how the APK arrived (FileOriginUrl / initiating process). 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the APK, isolate the device, and reset credentials for accounts used on it — BTMOB abuses Accessibility Services to steal logins and OTPs. 3) Hunt: correlate the device against the C2 network/URI detections (server.yaarsa.com, /yaarsa/private/), search mail/proxy for the delivery lure, and check for other endpoints holding any BTMOB sample hash.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Potato privilege-escalation tooling (GodPotato / SweetPotato / BadPotato) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — An analysis of incidents at Brazilian educational institutions
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-access batch script observed in the leaked-LockBit-builder case that enabled RDP by setting fDenyTSConnections to 0 and disabled endpoint defenses before ransomware deployment. Anchors on the exact registry value/data pair the article's script wrote. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim registry write from the article's disable-defenses batch script (HKLM\...\Control\Terminal Server \ fDenyTSConnections = 0) which turns RDP on; pairs it with reg.exe execution to keep fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-builder-leaked-online-by-angry-developer/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately enabling RDP on a new server build via a provisioning script
  • GPO/DSC/Intune configuration baseline that manages fDenyTSConnections
  • MSP onboarding automation that turns on RDP for remote management
  • Server 2016 role-setup wizards that toggle Remote Desktop
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","omadmclient.exe","gpscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating account and parent process of the reg.exe/registry write; confirm whether the same host also saw EDR/Defender service stops in the surrounding minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the account used to write the value, and re-set fDenyTSConnections to 1 if the change was unauthorized. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP (LogonType 10) and search for PsExecSvc.exe/named ransomware payloads (1.exe, LBB.exe) and Defender-tamper events fleet-wide.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Terminal Server"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "fDenyTSConnections"
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SystemSettings.exe","ServerManager.exe","mmc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| where CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections" and CommandLine has_any ("/d 0","/d 0x0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the manual lateral deployment of the custom LockBit build from the leaked builder: the sample was configured without psexec_netspread, so operators used PsExec (PsExecSvc.exe) to remotely launch ransomware binaries named 1.EXE and LBB.exe. Targets the impact/deployment step, not generic PsExec admin use. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim payload names (1.EXE, LBB.exe) and the PsExecSvc.exe service the operators relied on for manual spread after building a variant without psexec_netspread; combining parent + payload names keeps the otherwise-generic 1.exe fidelity acceptable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1486 T1569.002 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin using Sysinternals PsExec for remote software rollout (PsExecSvc.exe as parent)
  • Automation/RMM that names a tool 1.exe in a temp build path
  • Software packaging test binaries transiently named 1.exe
  • Remote patch scripts pushed via PsExec across a fleet
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\SCCM\\","\\ccmcache\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 and full path of the spawned binary and the source host driving PsExecSvc.exe; check for mass DeviceFileEvents FileRenamed/FileModified bursts on the same device. 2) Contain: network-isolate affected hosts, block the payload hash, and disable the deploying account. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where PsExecSvc.exe appeared (USN Journal .KEY artifacts corroborate historic spread), look for kill_defender/Defender-uninstall events and wallpaper/registry changes indicative of LockBit encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "PsExecSvc.exe"
    or FileName in~ ("1.exe","LBB.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\PsExecSvc.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\1.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\LBB.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potato privilege-escalation tooling (GodPotato / SweetPotato / BadPotato) AIExploitation High
Hunts the SeImpersonate token-abuse tools the article attributes to the observed privilege-escalation activity in these intrusions. Anchors on the exact tool family names used to move from a service/valid account to SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the three Potato variant names the article explicitly attributes to privilege escalation (GodPotato, SweetPotato, BadPotato); these are offensive-only tool names, so name/cmdline matches are high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/
ATT&CKT1134.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / pentest engagement running Potato tools with authorization
  • Security researcher detonating the tools in a sandbox VM
  • A file legitimately containing the substring 'potato' in an unrelated business name (rare, mitigated by path/cmdline context)
  • Malware-analysis training lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Tools\RedTeam\", @"\PurpleTeam\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating (pre-escalation) account and whether the resulting process/child ran at SYSTEM integrity; review parent process (often a service or web-app pool identity). 2) Contain: isolate the host and reset credentials for the abused service/valid account. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for follow-on SYSTEM-level actions — Defender-disable batch scripts, RDP enablement (fDenyTSConnections=0), PsExec spread, and ransomware payload drops.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
    or CommandLine has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the attacker-driven AnyDesk deployment the article ties to DragonForce (Case 02): AnyDesk installed and configured for unattended access to give operators remote control before ransomware. Anchors on the unattended-install command-line flags rather than mere presence of AnyDesk. Rationale: Anchors on AnyDesk (named in Case 02 as the DragonForce remote-access vector) combined with unattended-install flags that legitimate interactive users rarely pass, corroborated by DragonForce write-ups documenting silent AnyDesk installs for persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/dragonforce-ransomware-attack/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1219 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk legitimately deploying AnyDesk unattended via GPO/RMM
  • MSP standardizing on AnyDesk for remote support with --start-with-win
  • User self-installing AnyDesk from a legit MSI that passes --silent
  • Vendor support session where AnyDesk is provisioned with a set password
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the installing account and parent process (deployment tool vs. email client vs. script) and whether AnyDesk is a sanctioned tool for this host/OU. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill AnyDesk, and rotate credentials; capture the AnyDesk ID/anydesk.trace for the incoming operator IP. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents for AnyDesk relay traffic (boot.net.anydesk.com / *.relay), then look for DragonForce indicators — PsExec spread, mass encryption, ransom notes — across hosts that ran AnyDesk in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AnyDesk.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password","--get-id")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AnyDesk Unattended/Silent Install
id: d4a2f915-3b67-4c88-a0e2-9c1b6f2e7a55
description: Detects AnyDesk executed with unattended-install / auto-start / password-set flags, matching the attacker-installed AnyDesk that preceded DragonForce deployment in the Brazilian educational institution incidents.

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\AnyDesk.exe OR *\\anydesk.exe OR *\\ANYDESK.EXE) @CommandLine:(*--install* OR *--silent* OR *--start-with-win* OR *--set-password*)

| CommandLine=/--(install|silent|start-with-win|set-password)/i

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="AnyDesk.exe" (Processes.process="*--install*" OR Processes.process="*--silent*" OR Processes.process="*--start-with-win*" OR Processes.process="*--set-password*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="AnyDesk.exe" (Processes.process="*--install*" OR Processes.process="*--silent*" OR Processes.process="*--start-with-win*" OR Processes.process="*--set-password*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chinese Threat Actor Uses Leaked DarkSword Kit to Deploy GHOSTBLADE on iOS

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor has been observed running a campaign targeting Apple iOS devices by leveraging a publicly leaked version of the DarkSword exploit kit. Attack surface management platform Censys said it identified the threat actor running more than 100 web properties, most of which are fake Amazon Web Services (AWS) sign-in pages on a domain that also hosts the exploit

ATT&CKT1190 T1566 T1566.002
Domainst.me/YATA0000
IPs38.181.52.95 103.106.190.217 38.22.89.117 103.97.128.67 162.4.136.30 223.26.63.56 151.243.126.191 107.175.49.181 103.238.129.112 103.226.155.200 103.226.155.201 202.8.120.249 93.152.221.37

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Browser web session to fake AWS-console / Apple ID DarkSword watering-hole hosts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE exploit-panel and C2 infrastructure IPs · [LLM] Proxy hunt for DarkSword operator Telegram contact channel t.me/YATA0000 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE exploit-panel and C2 infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control High
Alerts when any managed host (Windows/macOS endpoint, or an iOS/BYOD device traversing a corporate firewall or proxy) connects to the 13 Censys-identified DarkSword Admin, Decode Dashboard, and C2 Control Panel IPs that also host the GHOSTBLADE credential-exfil endpoints. This is the only honest way to surface an iOS DarkSword compromise on non-iOS telemetry — the implant's file/keychain/iCloud exfil sweep transits these hosts. Rationale: Uses the 13 concrete C2/exploit-panel IPs from the Censys/THN analysis (panels on :8888 and :3000, Decode Dashboard, C2 Control Panel co-hosting the Apple ID decoy, and the Frankfurt open-directory tooling host). Cross-checked against GTIG's DarkSword write-up confirming the kit/GHOSTBLADE family; IPs themselves trace to the single Censys source so keep at alerting-with-triage. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/darksword-ios-exploit-chain • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-darksword-ios-exploit-used-in-infostealer-attack-on-iphones/ • https://iverify.io/blog/darksword-ios-exploit-kit-explained
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Your own attack-surface/TI scanners (Censys, Shodan, RiskIQ agents) beaconing the same hosting IPs from a corporate egress range
  • Automated IOC-enrichment/sandbox tooling auto-resolving these indicators from a SOAR host
  • A shared-hosting IP being re-assigned to a benign tenant after takedown (validate the port and whether the panel front-end still responds)
  • Threat-intel researchers on the network manually browsing the exposed panels
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("censys-scanner.exe","nmap.exe","masscan.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SOAR\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and whether it is a Windows/macOS endpoint or an iOS/BYOD device on corp WiFi; check the initiating process and destination port (8888/3000 = admin panel access, 80/443 = phishing-page/exploit delivery). 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at the firewall/proxy, isolate the source device; for a suspected iOS victim, force an Apple ID password reset and revoke iCloud/keychain sessions (GHOSTBLADE dumps keychain, iCloud, and Wi-Fi creds). 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across DNS/proxy for the other 12 IPs and the t.me/YATA0000 operator channel, and review AAD/Apple ID sign-ins from anomalous geographies following the connection.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (DarkSwordIPs)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Attempts=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc

| order by LastSeen desc

Browser web session to fake AWS-console / Apple ID DarkSword watering-hole hosts AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces a corporate browser navigating to the DarkSword-operator IPs that serve fake AWS sign-in and Apple ID credential-harvesting pages hosting the malicious iframe that fires the exploit chain. Targets the initial-access step where an AWS admin or user is lured to the watering hole from a managed desktop before any iOS payload runs. Rationale: Article states the chain begins when a victim reaches an AWS-console impersonation subdomain or Apple ID sign-in page hosting the malicious iframe; scopes the delivery-side IPs (Singapore multi-front-end 38.181.52.95, Apple ID decoy 103.106.190.217, the six :8888/:3000 exploit panels) to browser-initiated sessions, distinguishing a lured user from generic egress. Corroborated by DarkReading/BleepingComputer on the Safari-page-load exploit vector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/darksword-iphone-exploit-spies-thieves • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-darksword-ios-exploit-used-in-infostealer-attack-on-iphones/
ATT&CKT1189 T1203
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security awareness/phishing-simulation platforms proxying users through the same hosting ranges
  • An analyst manually visiting the reported phishing page from a lab browser to validate takedown
  • Hosting IP re-assigned to a legitimate site after infrastructure takedown
  • URL-rewrite / SASE inspection appliances that re-fetch the page on the user's behalf
Suppression filter
| where SrcHostname !has "phish-sim" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser actually rendered the page (HTTP 200 in ImWebSession/RemoteUrl) vs a blocked SASE fetch, and identify the user and whether they hold AWS console or Apple ID access. 2) Contain: block the host at the web proxy, reset the user's AWS console + Apple ID credentials and revoke active sessions/tokens, and check for MFA-prompt fatigue on both. 3) Hunt: correlate the same user/device to any of the 13 infrastructure IPs and to subsequent AWS CloudTrail ConsoleLogin / Apple ID sign-ins from unusual geographies within 24h.
let PhishHosts = dynamic(["38.181.52.95","103.106.190.217","38.22.89.117","103.97.128.67","162.4.136.30","223.26.63.56","151.243.126.191","107.175.49.181","103.238.129.112"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari","arc.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteIP in (PhishHosts)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (PhishHosts)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Proxy hunt for DarkSword operator Telegram contact channel t.me/YATA0000 AICommand & Control Low
Low-volume, high-precision hunt for any host in the estate reaching the DarkSword operator's recovered Telegram contact channel (t.me/YATA0000), the only direct operator comms channel Censys recovered from the 亚太集团 (Asia-Pacific Group) C2 Control Panel. A hit indicates either operator activity from inside the estate or a device negotiating an out-of-band exfil/comms path. Rationale: Uses the exact operator contact string hxxps://t[.]me/YATA0000 that Censys rendered from the 亚太集团 C2 Control Panel — the single direct operator channel recovered. Near-zero legitimate traffic to this specific Telegram path makes it a high-precision (if low-volume) hunt; Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as they lack full-URL-path proxy telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/chinese-threat-actor-uses-leaked.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1102
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel analyst clicking the reported Telegram link during research
  • Automated URL detonation/sandbox following the IOC
  • A Telegram deep-link that legitimately resolves the same handle after the channel is repurposed
  • URL-preview/link-unfurl services in chat apps fetching the link
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/user and the process that generated the request (browser vs script/tool) and whether it was analyst research. 2) Contain: if non-research, isolate the host and block t.me/YATA0000 plus the associated C2 IP 103.106.190.217 at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host across the 13 DarkSword infrastructure IPs and review for prior watering-hole browser sessions and credential-exfil egress.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "YATA0000" or RemoteUrl has_all ("t.me","YATA0000")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "YATA0000"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstIpAddr, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-03 10 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Explore how passkey implementation gaps undermine security when relying parties fail to validate the User Verified flag, reducing MFA to a single factor. The post Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1555.003 T1566 T1574.002
